searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, one left unspent, none of them the author's. Nine were restricted to a house's own domain (chateauducedre.com twice, brumont.fr twice, jurancon-cauhape.com twice, tirecul-la-graviere.fr, vins-plageoles.com) or to the INAO (inao.gouv.fr, the six first appellations) and are read as primary through their summaries; the other eighteen went to the open web for the second source of a date, a person, a decree or a method, two of them to the ministry's and the INAO's cahiers through their summaries. No WebFetch was tried. Every record was tested; no fact that rests on no source was kept.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the houses' own pages for their own dates and methods, then to the appellation texts (the Cahors wine body, the INAO, the ministry's cahiers for Madiran, Jurançon and Gaillac), then to the open web for the second source of each date, person and method.

Where a house's sheet and later accounts disagree on a method (Montus's barrels since 2017, Le Cèdre's casks by vintage) the record gives the house's figure as its sheet's and the later change without a figure; where two accounts disagree on who or when (the Plageoles organic turn) the record gives neither.

Sources whose title or address names a living person (iDealwine's Le Cèdre Blanc listings carrying the brothers' names, the Guide Hachette's page for the Plageoles company, a vertical tasting on the Montus site under a critic's name, a wine wiki on a writer's own site) were read in the results but never cited here; the fragment's own sources were left as the author wrote them, save two replaced (Sud Ouest France by Vinous for Montus, a merchant's sheet by the ministry's cahier for Cauhapé).

tested: The history (1958, the lavender, 1973, 1987): the estate's history page through search and Vintage and Vine; the couple, the first hectare beside the lavender, the first bottling of 1973 while still distilling, confirmed; the sons came home in 1987 when the father fell ill: changed.

The white: Le Cèdre Blanc, Viognier, IGP Côtes du Lot in three listings: the trap changed.

The questions: one key each, the distractors of one kind; the explanation of the wine question reworded. The house rules: nobody living named (the sons and the couple described), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash.

changed.was: Ondenc, Prunelart, Verdanel and Len de l'El came back to their own ground, and the domaine grows fourteen historic grapes of Gaillac, seven of them of the Mauzac family, beside a collection kept to save them. The next generation took the vines to organic farming, and the one after it has followed.
changed.now: Ondenc, Prunelart and Verdanel among them came back to their own ground. The estate went on to farm all its vines organically, and a younger generation of the family has since taken up the work.
changed.why: Len de l'El is in one guide's list of grapes the family replanted but no source names it among the lost, while iDealwine names Mauzac, Ondenc, Verdanel, Duras and Prunelart as the grapes saved. The fourteen grapes rest on one guide and the seven of the Mauzac family and the collection on none read, so they are cut. The organic turn is credited to the son by one account and to the early 1990s by another (Ecocert from 2007 by a third), so it is undated and unattributed; the estate's own sheet says all its vines are farmed organically, and two accounts have the grandsons running the domaine.
